Chapter 205 "Hey, buddy." He said. "Dad. The varied thrush was there again." Noah said. "Four days?" He said. "Four days. I think it's decided to stay for a while. Mom says some birds do that - they find a place that has what they need and they stay longer than expected." Noah said. "Your mom is right." He said. "I know. She's right about birds." Noah said. He said it with the specific confidence of someone whose primary research consultant had a reliable track record. "Are you ready for tomorrow?" He said. "The panel?" Noah said. "Yes." Noah said. "I'm not on the panel." Noah said. "I know.

I meant are you ready for it to happen." He said. Noah thought about this. "Yes," he said. "I think the best thing that can happen is that you both say smart things and the people in the room learn something. That would be a good day." "That's a good way to think about it." He said. "I know." Then: "Also, Dad. She packed the good coat." Noah said. "The charcoal one?" He said. "Yes. She always packs it for important things." Noah said. "Then it will be a good day." He said. Noah seemed satisfied. He went back to the varied thrush documentation. The call ended. He sat at the desk.

He thought about the charcoal coat and what it meant that Noah had reported it - not because Noah had been instructed to report it, but because Noah had assessed the information as relevant and had offered it with the matter-of-fact quality of someone making a useful contribution to an ongoing project. 7/3 +15 Bonus His son thought the charcoal coat was information he needed. His son was not wrong. He did the David Okonkwo call. He reviewed the Q4 projections with the focused attention they deserved. He handled the three emails that had been waiting since the board call.

He did the ordinary work of a Thursday afternoon when the extraordinary thing was tomorrow. In the evening he read for two hours. Not the panel prep material - he had done that, it was done, reading it again would be performance rather than preparation. He read what he was reading, which was a history of the railroad expansion in the American West that he had found in November and had been working through with genuine interest. He cooked dinner. He ate at the desk. He picked up the Cannon Beach photograph.

He had moved it from his phone wallpaper to a print - a decision made in September when he realised he wanted something physical, something that existed in the room rather than only on a screen. It sat on the corner of his desk where he could see it from any angle. Ethan at Haystack Rock. The hand raised. The grey Oregon sky. "Tomorrow." He said. He looked at the photograph for a while. "I'm going to be in a room with her and I'm going to say what I think about legal technology and I'm going to listen to what she says and I'm going to be exactly who I have been building.

That's all." He paused. "You would have had opinions about the panel topic. Very specific opinions. You would have presented them at breakfast before I left and you would have been right about most of them." He said. He set the photograph down. He went to bed. He did not lie awake thinking about tomorrow. He had, somewhere in the fourth year, developed the capacity to put significant things down before sleep and pick them up in the morning - not suppression, the actual resting of a mind that had learned it did not have to process everything continuously. He put tomorrow down. He slept.

In the morning he ran his usual eight kilometres. He came back and showered and made coffee and stood at the window. 2/3 Chunter 205 +15 Bonus Chicago at six AM in October. The lake doing what it did, the city beginning its day with the competence that had always been there regardless of what he was doing or not doing. He had been watching Chicago from windows for a long time. He had not always deserved the view. He put on his suit. He picked up the Cannon Beach photograph and looked at it once more. He put it in the inside pocket of his jacket.

Not the letters - those lived in the jacket always. The photograph was new. He wanted to carry it today. He wanted Ethan in his pocket on the day when he was going to be in the same room as his mother, building together in public, the best part of both of them, as Noah had said. He went. Chapter 206 She told Ethan she was wearing the charcoal coat. - Not the photograph on the mantelpiece - the one in Portland, the one she said good morning to every day. She was in the Chicago hotel room with a different photograph: the one she had printed and put in the inner compartment of her travel bag two years ago, the one from the tidepool at Cannon Beach, the ranger and Ethan both crouched over something beautiful, his face entirely given over to the looking. She had been carrying it on every Chicago trip. She said: "Charcoal coat today. The good one.

Your brother told Dad and he's going to wear the good suit and apparently we both have things we wear for important things." She looked at the photograph. "I thought you'd find that funny. The parallel. You would have catalogued it. Added it to some internal system of observations about how people reveal themselves through their outerwear choices." She put the photograph back in the bag. She stood at the hotel window. Chicago at six-forty AM.

The lake on the eastern horizon doing what October lakes did, the city below her beginning its complicated Friday morning, the specific quality of a large thing that had its own momentum and did not require her to participate in order to continue. She had been standing at hotel windows in Chicago for two weeks. She was almost done being afraid of this city. Not afraid - that was the wrong word. She had not been afraid of Chicago. She had been afraid of what Chicago meant, which was different. Chicago meant the ten years. The marriage. The supply closet at St.

Michael's and the emerald dress and seventeen missed calls and the CICU corridor. Chicago meant the departure - the night she had driven out of the city with two bags and a plan and a grief that had not yet finished arriving. She was not afraid of any of that anymore. She had walked the old neighborhood and had stood at the apartment window box and had been to the grave and had sat in the State Street coffee shop for an hour and twelve minutes and she had not been overcome by any of it.

She had simply been there, in those places, feeling what they contained and finding that the feeling was survivable, She had survived unsurvivable things. Coffee shops were well within her capacity. She made the hotel coffee. She sat at the desk. She looked at the conference programme on her 173 En apter 200 +15 Bonus laptop - Section Four, Friday afternoon, two PM. Four panellists. Forty-five minutes. Three hundred people. She was not anxious about the panel. That was the thing she was noting with the attention she gave things that were true and unexpected. She was not anxious.

She had prepared - she knew the material completely, had been building in this space for ten years and had, since the IPO, been the most visible person in it. She could do this panel in her sleep. She had also prepared for the specific configuration of the panel, which was the consideration she had been giving it since Monday: what it meant to be on a stage with him, how to conduct herself, what the room would be looking for. She had decided the room could look for whatever it wanted.

She was going to talk about legal technology with three people who knew the subject, and then she was going to leave, and the room could interpret the geometry of the panel however it chose to interpret it. She called Amara at seven. "Panel day." Amara said. "Panel day." She said. "How are you?" Amara said. "Clear." She said. "Not nervous?" Amara said. "Not about the panel." She said. "What about the other part?" Amara said. "I'm not nervous about that either. I was, until this week.

I came to Chicago thinking I was going to find out something and I was afraid of what I was going to find." She looked at the window. "I've been finding out things for two weeks. The findings are-" She paused." They're what they are. I'm not afraid of them." She said. "What are they?" Amara said. "That ordinary is possible. That he is who he has been building and it is not a performance." She paused. "That I am not the same person I was when I left this city and neither is he and those two people might be able to do something that the two people who were here before couldn't." She said.

Chapter 207 Amara was quiet for a moment. Then: "Sophia." "I know." She said. "Are you going to tell him?" Amara said. "I don't know yet. There's something I've been carrying for a couple of days. A piece of paper. I wrote something down on Wednesday night after the grave and I've been carrying it." She said. "What does it say?" Amara said. "I'll tell you after." She said. She got dressed. The charcoal coat over the dark dress she had brought for professional occasions. The watch she wore when the day required her to be the full version of herself.

She checked the mirror not for vanity but for confirmation - the specific check of a person who wanted to know that what they presented was consistent with who they were. It was consistent. She put the photograph back in the inner compartment of her bag. She put the piece of paper in the left pocket of the coat - the pocket closest to her chest, which was where she had always carried things she intended to act on. She walked to the conference centre.

She had chosen to walk rather than take a car because the morning was clear and the distance was twelve minutes and she needed the twelve minutes to be moving rather than stationary. She walked through Chicago with the specific attention she had been giving the city since she arrived - not nostalgia, not catalogue, just looking at what was there. The city was what it was. She had left it and she had come back and it was still what it was.

That was the truth of cities and the truth of people you had known a long time and the truth of anything that had its own substance independent of your presence or absence. She arrived at the conference centre nine minutes before she needed to be there. She stood in the lobby. She looked across it before she was fully oriented to the space. A reflex - she had always scanned rooms on arrival, the specific instinct of someone who processed spaces before she processed the people in them. She was not looking for him. She was looking at the room. 1:3 Chraper 2017 +15 Bonus She found him anyway.

He was on the far side of the lobby, near the registration tables. He was in conversation with the conference organizer - she could see the lanyard, the specific posture of someone conducting a professional courtesy exchange. He was in the good suit, as Noah had predicted. The dark one, the one that did not announce itself. He had not seen her yet. She stood still. She gave herself ten seconds.

In the ten seconds she looked at him across the lobby of the Chicago Legal Technology Conference on a Friday morning in October and she held what she felt with the attention she gave things she needed to understand. What she felt: recognition. Not the recognition of someone familiar in the shallow sense - she had always recognised him, had spent five years recognizing his absence. The recognition of someone who had gone away and returned and been found to be still themselves. He was still himself.

A different version of himself, the better version she had been watching become real for two weeks, but the same underneath in the ways that mattered. She also felt something that did not have a clean name. Something that occupied the space between recognition and the thing that came after recognition when the recognised thing was also something you had not stopped wanting even during the years you had been telling yourself it was unavailable. Ten seconds. He turned. He saw her.

There was a moment - neither of them moved, the lobby continuing around them, the specific suspended quality of two people across a space recognising each other properly for the first time in five years - and in that moment she understood what the piece of paper in her pocket said and whether she was going to take it out. She was going to take it out. Not now. Not in the lobby. Later, when the ordinary thing she had been trying had had enough time to confirm itself. She crossed the lobby. 2/3 Charter 255 "Good morning." She said. "Good morning." He said.

The managing partner arrived second and went directly to the coffee urn, which was the correct priority. He arrived third. The academic and the managing partner were absorbed in their respective preparations. He and Sophia were at the end of the table.

He poured her coffee because the urn was on his side and she had just sat down and it was simply the available useful thing. She looked up from the notes she was reviewing. She said: "Which part?" "The part where we're both sitting in a greenroom before a legal technology panel pretending to be thinking about legal technology." He said. She looked at him for a moment.

"We are thinking about legal technology." She said. "A little." He said. "A little." She said. There it was - the almost-smile, the shape of it, the corner of her mouth moving in the direction it moved when something had landed correctly and she had not quite decided to let it land all the way. It was the same one she had almost produced when Amara made her almost-laugh in December of year 1/3 +15 Bonus one.

Something in the room shifted. Not dramatically - the academic was still in the corner, the managing partner was still at the coffee urn.

The quality of the air between them shifted in the specific way it shifted when two people had been carefully maintaining the appropriate distance and had, just briefly, stopped maintaining it. "He would have been remarkable." He said. "He was remarkable." She said. "Yes." He said. She looked at her notes. He looked at his. The greenroom continued around them with its adequate coffee and its wifi and its twelve minutes becoming ten. She said, without looking up: "I have something in my pocket. I've been carrying it since Wednesday." "Okay." He said. "I'm not going to take it out now.

We have a panel." She said. "Okay." He said. "I might take it out later. I haven't decided." She said. "Okay." He said. She looked up at him. "You keep saying okay." The almost-smile resolved itself into something - not the full version, but closer to full than almost. Not a smile exactly. Chapter 209 "I think that framing misses something important. The question isn't whether Al can perform legal research - it clearly can. The question is what legal judgment requires that Al currently can't replicate. The firms that are asking the first question are building for last year's problem. The ones asking the second question are building for next year's." She said. The managing partner, to his credit, acknowledged the point. "The challenge is that 'what legal judgment requires' is a question that changes as the technology changes.

Five years ago we would have said AI couldn't perform reliable case synthesis. Now it can, reasonably. The line keeps moving. Firms that are asking 'what can't AI do' today need to be ready for the answer to be different in three years." He said. She looked at him. He looked at her. Ms. Kane arguing that firms The moderator said: "That's an interesting point of tension should focus on what AI can't replicate, Mr. Kane suggesting that the boundary of what AI can't do is itself moving. Ms. Kane, do you want to respond?" "Yes. I think we're actually agreeing.

The firms that will survive aren't the ones that have found the current boundary and sat down behind it. They're the ones that understand why the boundary keeps moving and are building the capacity to keep pace with the movement." She paused. "Which is another way of saying that the question isn't about the technology. It's about the institutional capacity to keep asking the right questions." She said. "That's a better formulation than mine." He said. She said, to the room rather than to him: "It builds on his." The room noticed.

Three hundred legal technology professionals noticed the exchange and filed it in the specific way rooms filed things they had not expected. He could feel the noticing without looking at the audience. He did not look at the audience. He looked at the moderator, who was moving the panel forward with the professional aplomb of someone who had just witnessed something unexpected and had decided the best response was to continue. The moderator had allowed it because the quality of the discussion had warranted the extension. Not by arrangement - the moderator directed questions to specific panellists and twice the direction landed on both of them and 1/3 +15 Bonus they answered in sequence, building from each other's responses the way the grave-visit conversation had built, the way the State Street conversation had built. She had been at the hotel desk at ten PM with the day in her - the stone and the cold and his voice reading the letters and what she had said at the end, at the cars, about why she had really come back. She had sat down and she had written it without managing it, which meant it had come out exactly true rather than exactly right, which she had learned were not always the same thing. She read it now. She had read it three times since she wrote it.

The reading was not revision - she was not going to revise it, had decided that on the second reading when she understood that revising it would turn it into a managed version, which was the thing she had been done with for five years. She was reading it to confirm that it was still true. It was still true. "The panel was good." She said. "I knew it would be." He said.

"You were right about the working together part." She said. "I know." He said it without smugness, the way he said most true things - simply, because they were true and there was no reason to elaborate on the truth. "Was it the best part of you? " He said. She thought about it. "Yes," she said. "I think it was." 1/3 +15 Bonus He seemed satisfied. "I'm having dinner with him tonight." She said. Noah was quiet for a moment. People go back to the same place when the first time was good." He paused. "I learned that from the Bird Guide. Birds do it too." He said. "You're three and a half." she said. "Almost four." He said. "Noah. I have something I'm going to give him tonight. I wrote it down." She said. "What is it?" He said. "Something true." She said. He thought about this. "True things are the right things to give people." He said. "Yes." She said. "Mom. I love you." He said. "I love you too, bug." She said. "Tell me what happens. Not tonight - I'll be asleep. But in the morning." He said.

"I'll call you in the morning." She said. She ended the call. She sat at the desk with the piece of paper. She thought about what it said and whether it was the right thing to give him. Not whether it was true - she had confirmed that. Whether it was right. Whether this was the moment, and this was the form, and whether the last six years of working out who she was and what she wanted had arrived at a conclusion that was clean enough to say. It was clean enough. She had not arrived at it easily.

She had arrived at it through Portland and Noah and LexNova and two years of Ryan being present and patient and honest with her and six months of 2/3 +15 Bonus Chicago trips and a grave on a Saturday and a coffee shop on a Thursday and a conference room on a Friday afternoon where they had built an argument together in front of three hundred people and it had been the best part of both of them. She had arrived at it. She put the piece of paper back in the coat pocket. She put the coat on. She walked to State Street.

The evening was the specific quality of October in Chicago when the season had committed: cold without cruelty, the air clear and dark, the city doing what it did in its evening mode which was to be slightly less purposeful than it was in the day and slightly more itself. Chapter 211 "It applies to more than legal technology." She said. "I know." He said. - no, not She looked at the courtyard. The October dark beyond the window. The cedar fence Portland, Chicago, the courtyard with the specific Chicago autumn quality of a space that had been maintained through everything and intended to continue. She put her hand in the coat pocket. She took out the piece of paper. She set it on the table between them. "I wrote this on Wednesday. After the grave. I've been carrying it." She said. He looked at it. He did not reach for it. "You can read it." She said.

He picked it up. He unfolded it with the care he used for things that had been folded with intention. He read it. She watched him read. The piece of paper said: I don't need you. I built everything I needed. I have a son who knows what birds mean and a company I made from nothing and a foundation that finds children before the finding comes too late.
